author: Kiara Green
title: What Rights Are at Stake in the Supreme Court’s 2026-27 Term?
content:
The US Supreme Court reconvened on October 5 for its 2026-27 term which concludes in June of 2027. Cases involving the rights of immigrants, rules governing elections, LGBTQIA rights, and more, stand at the forefront this term. The Court’s decisions could have significant consequences for how federal and state laws protect individual rights.

The Court begins this term with a 6–3 conservative majority. Three of the nine justices, Neil Gorsuch, Brett Kavanaugh, and Amy Coney Barrett, were nominated by President Donald Trump. Recent decisions, including the overturning of Dobbs and rulings affecting the enforcement of the Voting Rights Act, have already reshaped the legal landscape. This term, the justices will consider additional disputes over voting regulations and the rights of young people.

Among these cases is Republican National Committee v. Mi Familia Vota, which is scheduled to be heard on December 8. The Court will decide whether Arizona can require proof of citizenship to register to vote and if the National Voter Registration Act prohibits Arizona from canceling the registrations of non-citizens within 90 days of a federal election.

author: Giovanna DeStefanis
title: A Student’s Guide to Protecting Your Vote on Election Day
content:
As the November 3 midterm elections approach next week, knowing your voting rights and how to respond at the polls is essential to protecting access to the ballot. For students voting on campus or in their local communities, possibly for the first time, it can be particularly confusing when state laws differ or voting procedures are unfamiliar.

Every eligible voter deserves the opportunity to cast a ballot freely, privately, and without intimidation. Here is what voters need to know before heading to the polls.

Federal and state laws protect voters against various forms of discrimination, intimidation and interference. Knowing your rights can help you recognize when to ask for assistance.

You have the right to equal treatment. Federal law prohibits discrimination in voting on protected grounds, including race and color. Other federal and state laws, such as the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) and Section 208 of the Voting Rights Act, provide additional protections related to accessible polling places and language assistance. Voters who need assistance due to disability or difficulty reading/writing English have the right to bring a person of their choice into the voting booth to assist them, as long as that person is not their employer or union representative.

Your voting choices are yours alone and you should not be forced to disclose your selections or pressured to vote for a particular candidate.

You have the right to vote without intimidation or coercion. Threats, harassment and certain other efforts to interfere with voting are prohibited under federal law (18 U.S.C. § 594) and state election codes.

What to Do if Your Name Is Missing From the Voter List

If a poll worker cannot find your name on the voter registration list, do not immediately assume you are ineligible to vote.

Ask the poll worker to verify your registration information. Corfim whether you are at the correct precinct and polling location and whether a spelling discrepancy, name change or other registration issue could explain the problem.

Check if your state has Same-Day Voter Registration or Election Day Registration. 20 states and Washington, DC, allow eligible voters to register and cast a ballot on the spot with proof of identity and residency (such as a student ID paired with a campus housing statement or utility bill). In this case, you should ask to register and vote in the same visit.

Under the Help America Vote Act (HAVA) of 2002, if you affirm that you are registered and eligible in that jurisdiction, poll workers are required to offer you a provisional ballot in federal elections. Note that Idaho, Minnesota, and New Hampshire do not issue provisional ballots, but they offer in-person Election Day Registration to all voters.

What to Do If the Line is Too Long

Long lines at polling stations near college campuses are common, but long waits should never prevent you from casting your ballot.

Stay in line! If you are in line when the polls officially close, you have the legal right to vote. Election officials are required by law to keep the polling location open until every voter who was in line by the closing deadline has cast their ballot. Do not leave the line.

If the lines are moving unusually slowly, report the issue immediately to your local county election office or the Election Protection Hotline (866-OUR-VOTE).

If you are voting on Election Day, bring a valid photo ID, water, snacks, a fully charged phone, and any voting notes to help.

If FBI, ICE or Other Federal Agents Appear at a Polling Place

The presence of federal law enforcement can create fear and confusion, particularly for marginalized and student communities. Under federal law (including 18 U.S.C. § 592), it is illegal for federal military personnel or armed federal agents, including ICE, FBI, or U.S. Marshals, to be stationed at or monitor polling places to interfere with an election or intimidate voters. The DOJ is claiming that ICE won’t patrol the polls, but it is important to know your rights and what to do to ensure your vote is protected.

Always remain calm and keep your hands visible at all times. Don’t physically resist or obstruct law enforcement. Ask: “Am I free to go?” If the answer is yes, walk away calmly and proceed to vote. If an official requests to search you, you have the right to say no, but do not obstruct access. For additional security, turn off biometric identification such as Face ID.

Record the time, badge numbers, agency names, vehicle descriptions, and exact actions taken by officers or agents, provided it is safe to do so.

If you see an official or witness an encounter, report it immediately. Notify the chief election judge at the polling place, call local nonpartisan voter protection hotlines, and report the incident to the Election Protection Coalition.

Federal agents cannot demand identification from voters without reasonable suspicion of a crime. However, if you have been arrested while attempting to vote, you can exercise your right to remain silent and ask for a lawyer regardless of your citizenship or immigration status. To invoke these rights, say “I want to remain silent” and “I want to speak with a lawyer” and wait until you have a lawyer present.

Non-citizen family members or allies accompanying voters should be aware of their rights, but all voters have the right to cast their ballot without harassment.

Election Safety and Voting Rights Resources

Voters do not have to navigate election-related concerns alone. The Election Protection Coalition is a nonpartisan coalition that helps voters understand their rights, resolve voting problems, and find accurate election information. Its trained volunteers provide assistance throughout the voting process.

English: 866-OUR-VOTE (866-687-8683)

Spanish and English: 888-VE-Y-VOTA (888-839-8682)

Asian languages and English: 888-API-VOTE (888-274-8683)

Arabic and English: 844-YALLA-US (844-925-5287)

Democracy is strongest when every eligible voter, including students, can freely cast their ballot. As election deadlines quickly approach, take time to verify your registration, map out your voting plan, and share these rights with your peers. Protect your vote, look out for your community, and never hesitate to demand access to the ballot that federal and state laws guarantee.

For campus and state voting information, visit https://voteu.org/guides. For legal guidance on federal interference, visit: https://www.aclu.org/know-your-rights/federal-agents-at-the-polls.

author: FMF Staff
title: Deporting Afghans to the Taliban by Way of Pakistan Is a Betrayal That Gets the United States Nothing
content:
The Trump administration is reportedly preparing to put more than 150 Afghans on a flight to Pakistan, where they would then be transferred across the border into Taliban-ruled Afghanistan. AfghanEvac, a coalition advocating for Afghan allies, says some of those facing removal are the brothers and sons of men who served alongside U.S. forces. The first flight could leave as early as Monday, just one day before Election Day in the United States.

Because the United States cannot deport people directly to Afghanistan, it lacks official diplomatic relations with the Taliban regime; the plan routes them through Pakistan. Call it what it is: a deportation to the Taliban with a layover. Officials reportedly told The New York Times that the removal is, in effect, to Afghanistan, and detainees have been told the same. Pakistan’s role is to carry out the handoff.

What the layover adds is risk. Afghans would be moved through a third country and beyond any oversight, and placed in the hands of authorities who have no obligation to protect them. From there, they could be pushed across the border to a regime they fled and one that would seek to harm them. These are the people who escaped Taliban rule after August 15, 2021.

Pakistan is not safe for Afghans. Since 2023, the Pakistani government has expelled over 2.4 million Afghan refugees back to Afghanistan as relations with the Taliban have deteriorated. Earlier this year, Pakistani officials ordered law enforcement agencies nationwide to arrest Afghans without valid visas. This is part of a years-long campaign of forced returns that has sent millions of Afghans back to a country where many face homelessness and unemployment. Many of those Afghan refugees were born and raised in Pakistan.

The Taliban’s “amnesty” is empty words. It is not a guarantee of safety.

On its first day back in power in August 2021, the Taliban announced a general amnesty for Afghans who worked with Western-backed forces and the former republic government of Afghanistan. That promise was never kept. The United Nations has documented reports of extrajudicial killings, arbitrary detentions, and other abuses. The families of former U.S. partners have particular reason to fear for their safety.

The policy to return Afghans to Afghanistan also lends credibility to the Taliban.

When the United States sends people into Taliban-controlled Afghanistan, even through a middleman, it implies that returning is safe. It suggests that the United States is willing to rely on the assurances of a regime that has repeatedly broken its promises and violated fundamental rights. Deporting Afghans in this way serves the Taliban’s desire to be treated as a legitimate government and to establish normal relations with the Trump administration.

The Trump administration advanced a similar narrative last year in May, when it ended temporary protections for Afghans, claiming that “Afghanistan has had an improved security situation” despite clear evidence to the contrary.

Cooperating, even indirectly, with a regime that has barred half the population of Afghanistan – girls and women – from education and public life, and has violated every international and national law gains the United States nothing in return. It is neither smart nor logical. It would not serve the U.S. now or in the future. It adds to the humiliation of how the U.S. withdrew from Afghanistan and handed the country back to the Taliban, a terrorist group it fought for 20 years.

The United States gains nothing from this policy. It loses far more.

The cost of this policy lands on American credibility. The United States asked Afghans to translate, guard, drive, gather intelligence, cook, clean, implement the many projects, and fight beside its forces, and promised to stand by them. Abandoning those allies, or their families, breaks that promise and abandons its obligation to protect people who are in harm’s way because they supported the U.S. mission.

The damage goes beyond Afghanistan. Future partners in any other conflict will remember how the United States treated those who stood with it. This is not border security. These individuals have already undergone vetting. It does not make Americans safer. It uses federal resources to send people toward danger, and abandons those who trusted the United States.

63% of Americans do not want Afghans to be deported.

A bipartisan national poll by AfghanEvac and HIAS, designed and run by Lake Research Partners and The Tarrance Group, found that 84 percent of likely 2026 voters say America should keep its promise to Afghan wartime allies. By more than two to one, voters oppose deporting hundreds of Afghan refugees who assisted U.S. forces to third countries where they have no connection, and 63 percent oppose deporting Afghan allies to such countries. Seventy-six percent support restoring protection programs for Afghans whose resettlement cases were already approved. Support for admitting Afghan allies rises from 52 percent to 72 percent once voters learn who these partners are.

Call your Member of Congress and your two senators. The Capitol switchboard is (202) 224-3121. Ask the operator to connect you with your Member’s office. Ask them to:

Publicly oppose this deportation flight and press the administration to halt removals of Afghans from the U.S.

Ask them to sign the discharge petition for the bipartisan Afghanistan TPS Act, which would protect Afghans already in the U.S.

Keep the promises made to Afghans who stood with us.

A simple script: I’m a constituent. I’m calling to ask [Member’s name] to oppose deporting Afghans to the Taliban through Pakistan and to protect Afghans who are already in the United States. Keeping our word to our allies is not only the right thing to do, it’s also a smart thing to do. We must deliver on our promise.

The United States made a promise. For 20 years, Afghan allies delivered, risking their lives and putting their families in danger in support of the U.S. mission in Afghanistan. The American people continue to stand with the Afghans who are already in the U.S. They believe it’s the right thing to honor its commitments. Deporting Afghans is not a sound policy, does not advance U.S. interests, and will only undermine America’s credibility.

For more on Afghan deportation, follow AfghanEvac here and here.

Source: AfghanEvac; the New York Times; Amu TV; USCIS.

author: Madelyn Amos
title: ¡Sí Se Puede!: Dolores Huerta’s Feminist Legacy Lives On
content:
Dolores Huerta, the pioneering labor leader, civil rights activist, and feminist who devoted her life to advancing equality and justice, has died at the age of 96. Her groundbreaking work reshaped the labor and feminist movements, leaving an enduring legacy of grassroots organizing, women’s leadership, and collective action that continues to inspire generations.

Huerta was a dear friend and ally of the Feminist Majority Foundation since its founding. She served on the organization’s board for more than 30 years, offering her passion, energy, and visionary leadership to the fight for gender equality.

In the 1980s, Feminist Majority co-founders Eleanor Smeal and Kathy Spillar recruited Huerta to join the Feminization of Power campaign to increase women’s representation in elected office. For four years, Huerta traveled across the country with the Feminist Majority. She mentored women running for office, particularly Latinas and other women of color, and helped them secure endorsements while campaigning alongside them.

Reflecting on their work together, Smeal recalled, “We traveled to 8 states and she was determined to change the composition of California’s state legislature — and she did. When we started the campaign in 1987, the state legislature was only 14.2% women, but because of Dolores, it quickly jumped to 24.2%. And today, the California legislature is 49.2% women.” No

author: Sara Fayyazi
title: Making Women’s History Part of the Curriculum
content:
Two teachers from Sacred Heart Preparatory School in California, Kristen Kelly and Serene Williams, have proposed an Advanced Placement U.S. Women’s History course in response to the issue of students not learning about women’s history. The courses would allow studying women’s experiences and contributions in greater depth. Establishing this course would create a better understanding of American history as it includes the diverse experiences of women and would help students connect the historical struggles for equality to gender issues today.

Women have contributed to shaping the nation’s politics, economy, and social movements, yet their participation is often overlooked by traditional history classes. From fighting for the right to vote, challenging discrimination, and advocating for female autonomy, women have had a significant role in building the foundation of the United States today.

One of the main arguments for WAPUSH is that women’s experiences are not explored in the classroom. In the article Educational Activism: Creating an AP U.S. Women’s History Course, Serene Williams, Kristen Kelly, and Clara Robinson explain that topics such as women’s suffrage and reproductive rights receive limited attention in the current AP U.S. History curriculum. author: Arezu Fayyazi
title: Domestic Violence and Femicide in Afghanistan: Women Are Denied Protection and Justice
content:
Domestic violence has intensified under Taliban rule since August 2021, as the regime has imposed more than 160 edicts and directives restricting the rights and freedoms of women and girls. By barring women from education and employment, severely limiting their freedom of movement, and denying them meaningful access to justice, the Taliban has deepened women’s dependence on their families and left many with fewer ways to escape abuse or seek protection. In this climate of systemic oppression and impunity, domestic violence can go unchallenged, while women and girls face the devastating risk of femicide.

Reports from The Guardian and Zan Times have recorded 231 cases of femicide across just ten provinces -there are 34 provinces – in Afghanistan since 2021. However, it is important to note that these reports emphasized the fact that these cases of femicide do not represent all of the cases in the country since 2021, given the fact that it’s difficult to record these instances of domestic violence after the Taliban has removed avenues to report these crimes.

The Taliban has dismantled the Ministry of Women’s Affairs, the prosecutor’s office that handled violence against women, and women’s shelters all together. author: Lillian Kollross
title: Texas Mother Sues Anti-Abortion Extremists Under Law Targeting Abortion Pills
content:
Last week, a Texas mother sued Kristan Hawkins, the president and founder of Students for Life of America, an anti-abortion organization, and three other staff members for breaking a law the group helped to establish.

In March 2026, Hawkins posted an Instagram photo with two other staff members in front of the Space Center Houston with the caption: “Guess what we are doing? Ordering abortion pills undercover? Yep. Stay tuned.”

The lawsuit was filed on Oct. 6 by Maria Puerto, who is using a pseudonym to protect her family. Ms. Puerto believes that the group violated House Bill 7, known as the Woman and Child Protection Act, and also mocked those Texans who were deeply affected by the bill.

In December 2025, the Texas legislature passed the Woman and Child Protection Act, which allows almost anyone to sue a person who imports, delivers, or prescribes abortion pills. Plaintiffs can win at least $100,000 per violation.

Despite being on birth control, in 2022, Puerto became pregnant. This unplanned pregnancy came right after Texas banned abortions. With no money or way to travel out of state, along with caring for her disabled mother, Puerto was unable to get an abortion and was forced to carry to term.

author: Sofia Little
title: Election Day is Not the Only Day to Vote
content:
October 24th is Vote Early Day, meant to encourage all eligible United States citizens to vote early and inform voters of their states’ early voting laws.

Early voting offers many voters the convenience and flexibility that match the demands of modern life. It can be especially helpful for people with demanding work schedules, long commutes, caregiving responsibilities or travel plans. For many, the option to vote early can make the difference between casting a ballot and missing the opportunity.

According to the Center for Election and Research (CEIR) nearly 97% of voting-age citizens live in states that offer at least one way to vote before Election Day.

However, access to the ballot remains a concern ahead of the 2026 midterm elections. The Trump administration has deployed a wide variety of intensified voter suppression tactics in an attempt to interfere with the 2026 midterm elections. These tactics range from plans to place federal officials at polling stations and an executive order targeting mail voting. Courts have blocked aspects of the administration’s mail voting order from taking effect.

The impact of these voter suppression maneuvers often harm communities of color. Strict voter ID laws and fewer polling locations in certain areas disproportionately affect voters of color, leading to longer wait times on Election Day and discriminatory intimidation tactics at

author: Kiara Green
title: Beyond Indigenous Peoples Day: The Fight to Protect Indigenous Communities
content:
The second Monday in October is federally recognized as Christopher Columbus Day, commemorating the arrival of colonizer Christopher Columbus to the Americas. It’s undeniable that Indigenous communities lived in America long before Columbus docked his ship. Why, then, is he celebrated as the man who “discovered” America?

For years, public debate has challenged this Eurocentric narrative. In response, several states have recognised the second Monday in October as Indigenous Peoples Day. The day celebrates the resilience and the vibrant cultures of Indigenous communities in America.

Despite the lack of federal recognition, Indigenous Peoples Day continues to be celebrated while bringing attention to issues that Indigenous communities face. The day has been used to advocate for the removal of Columbus memorials, the returning of Indigenous lands, and awareness about Missing and Murdered Indigenous Women (MMIW).

The Trump administration has rejected this broader recognition. In 2025, Trump declared he was “bringing Columbus Day back from the ashes,” reinforcing the federal emphasis on celebrating Columbus rather than recognizing Indigenous peoples.

author: Bianca Blell
title: Women and Girls Severely Affected in Colombia’s 7.4 Earthquake
content:
On August 10th, a magnitude 7.4 earthquake struck western Colombia, with its epicenter near San José del Palmar in the department of Chocó. It was the strongest earthquake recorded in the country in a decade. The disaster damaged homes and essential infrastructure across multiple departments, displacing residents and disrupting access to health care and other critical services.

Chocó, which has a large Afro-Colombian population, was among the hardest-hit areas. During this catastrophic tragedy, where 335 people died, 4,611 people were injured, and which left 111 people missing, it remains the country’s deadliest earthquake since the 1990s.

Though spread out through other nations and departments, most deaths occurred in Valle del Cauca and Risaralda, as the earthquake caused severe humanitarian and protection challenges for vulnerable populations, especially girls and women. More than 31,460 homes were destroyed. 4,996 community centers and 348 health facilities were affected due to conditions from the event. This large scale loss of housing, displacement, and disruption from essential networks have heightened risk of Gender-Based Violence (GBV), especially in rural communities.

In these communities, girls and women face heightened risks of exploitation, harassment, and sexual abuse due to the increase of displacement and chaos as a result of the earthquake. These risks can b

author: Halie Moses
title: The Z Factor: Young Voters and the 2026 Midterms
content:
Generation Z voters (aged 18-29) are predicted to make a significant impact on the upcoming 2026 Midterm elections. This has not always been the case, as student and youth voter turnout has historically remained low. Only 47% of Americans aged 18-29 voted in the 2024 election. This year, 50 million Gen Z Americans are eligible to vote.

In October, a report by UCLA’s William Institute examined the political priorities and voting intentions of Gen Z adults ahead of the 2026 midterms. The study found that nearly 74 percent of respondents said they were likely or certain to vote. These numbers come as no surprise to those who work with students, spend time organizing on college campuses, or identify as Gen Z during the Trump Administration. Rising living costs, ICE raids, attacks on reproductive rights access, sexual assault cases, climate change, and unwanted wars have directly impacted their lives and are driving them to the polls with a passion for change.

Leela Strong, Director of CIRCLE, who works to empower the youth vote, reflected: “Young people are sending us clear signals, not only of dissatisfaction with our politics and deep economic concerns, but also of a strong desire to take action and drive change.” Organizations such as When We All Vote are working to engage young people by connecting their priorities with the issues and candidates on their ballots. author: Marcelle Edenlord
title: California Takes Action to Address Housing Barriers for Survivors
content:
More than one in three women and one in six men in the United States have experienced sexual violence, physical violence and/or stalking by an intimate partner in their lifetime. For survivors trying to leave abusive relationships, finding safe, stable housing can be a major obstacle.

The Violence Against Women Act (VAWA), first enacted in 1994, established federal resources to address domestic violence and sexual assault. In the decades since, advocates and policymakers have worked to expand protections and services for survivors. However, access to these resources remains uneven, and recent reductions in federal funding have placed additional pressure on organizations that provide critical support.

From 2020 to 2024, violent crimes involving domestic relationships have increased by 1.9%, disrupting the consecutive decline in violence we saw in previous years. One factor we can attribute this to is the dramatic decline of the federal Victims of Crime Fund. This fund ensures countless crisis centers across the country serve their communities. In its depletion, the numbers speak for themselves.

So what are states doing about it?

author: Giovanna DeStefanis
title: JAWS Reception Celebrates Legacy of Women in Journalism
content:
The Journalism and Women Symposium (JAWS) celebrated the legacy of women journalists at a reception on October 2 hosted at the Ms. office. The gathering brought together journalists, longtime JAWS members, and feminist advocates to recognize the women who helped shape media and discuss the importance of preserving their work for future generations.

The reception highlighted the connections between JAWS, Ms. and the Feminist Majority Foundation (FMF), publisher of Ms. magazine. Kathy Bonk, a longtime feminist advocate and leader, recalled how Ms. founder Gloria Steinem reached out to ask FMF to keep the magazine alive. With the support of Ellie Smeal, Katherine Spillar, Peg Yorkin, and others, FMF committed to sustaining Ms. feminist journalism.

Bonk also reflected on the role of feminist journalism in advancing the women’s movement, arguing that the journalists who documented the movement helped make its progress possible. Bonk shared, “It’s no longer just news coverage. It’s looking for an impact. It’s looking at how we change people’s lives.”

A central focus of the reception was JAWS’ Legacy Fund and its efforts to preserve the history of women in journalism. Pam Morland, a former JAWS president and longtime journalist, described donating decades of professional and personal materials to archive her materials going back to 1985.

author: Jaharra Anglin Stubbs
title: Mail-In Ballots are Safe, For Now
content:
As early voting gets underway in many states, voters can continue to rely on existing mail-in voting procedures for the 2026 midterm elections. On September 14, the US Supreme Court declined to allow the Trump administration to implement new restrictions that would have given the USPS a greater role in determining which voters could receive mail-in ballots. The decision left a lower court order blocking the restrictions in place, allowing states to continue using their existing systems for the November election.

The ruling followed Trump’s Executive Order 14399, issued in March 2026, which took effect in August 2026. The Executive Order required states to adopt a “uniform envelope style” and to submit lists of eligible voters to an online portal. It gave the USPS the authority to refuse to deliver ballots to noncompliant states. In its appeal to the Supreme Court, the Trump administration argued that additional measures like this were needed to preserve election integrity, but that claim was disputed.

Concerns also emerged about whether the new system could function reliably before the midterm elections. A whistleblower report revealed that ballots may never be sent because of systemic and programmatic flaws. author: FMF Staff
title: ICC Arrest Warrants Challenge the Normalization of Taliban Rule and Gender Persecution
content:
On October 5, the International Criminal Court (ICC) unsealed arrest warrants for four senior Taliban officials. They include Taliban Supreme Leader Haibatullah Akhundzada, Chief Justice Abdul Hakim Haqqani, Education Minister Habibullah Agha, and Higher Education Minister Neda Mohammad Nadim. The warrants were issued in July 2025 but had remained sealed.

The ICC says there are reasonable grounds to believe the four are criminally responsible for the “crime against humanity of persecution on gender grounds against girls, women, and others who do not conform to the Taliban’s policies on gender, gender identity, or expression.” The crimes include conduct involving murder, imprisonment, torture, rape, and enforced disappearance.

The Court also found that Taliban decrees and edicts have severely deprived women and girls of fundamental rights, including education, privacy and family life, as well as freedoms of movement, expression, thought, conscience, and religion. Importantly, the Court recognized that gender persecution can encompass not only direct acts of violence, but also systemic and institutionalized forms of harm.

What does the arrest warrant mean for the four Taliban officials?

author: Marcelle Edenlord
title: Ovarian Cancer Awareness Month Has Ended, ​​But the Need for Research Remains
content:
September marked Ovarian Cancer Awareness Month, but the need for greater research, better treatment, and improved early detection does not end when the month does. Ovarian cancer is expected to cause nearly 14,000 deaths in the US this year. Despite the burden of the disease, detecting ovarian cancer early remains a significant challenge.

Ovarian cancer is actually the deadliest cancer among women and the number one cause of gynecologic cancer deaths. Additionally, only 15% of patients are diagnosed in early stages. Meaning the vast majority of individuals are diagnosed in advanced stages, their survival rate of 30.8%. This tragic reality is largely due to a lack of early detection testing.

Other cancers, such as breast cancer, have preventive measures, such as mammograms routinely recommended; so what’s preventing ovarian cancer from having similar life-saving services?

Breast cancer is the most funded women’s health condition, surpassing ovarian cancer funding levels by billions. Over a span of 25 years, the federal government funded prostate cancer 5.5 times more than ovarian cancer, allocating $276.5 million to the ovarian and $1.53 billion to the prostate.

author: Sofia Little
title: The Cornell 57: How Educational Institutions Fail Women
content:

On the night of October 19, 2024, a 20-year old Cornell University undergraduate student, identified as Jane Doe in court filings and media reports, went to the Chi Phi Fraternity house believing she was going to meet a friend. In a civil lawsuit filed in September 2026, Doe alleges that she was drugged and sexually assaulted by seven men over the course of several hours.

These are who the media have coined the ‘Cornell 7’: Matthew Ingalls, Jonathan Newell, Winston Lee, Gillio Lopes, Diego Sarabia, Scott Norris, and Scott Kretzschmar. The men have been accused of sexually assaulting Jane Doe, but they have not been criminally charged in connection with the allegations.

author: Giovanna DeStefanis
title: New Poll Finds Voters Concerned about Rights and Democracy Ahead of 2026 Midterms
content:
A new national poll from The Leadership Conference on Civil and Human Rights finds that voters are increasingly concerned about threats to their rights, democracy, and the 2026 elections. The 2026 Civil Rights Monitor found that 82% of voters are concerned that rights and freedoms are being taken away or rolled back, the highest level recorded in the five-year history of the poll.

The poll, conducted by Brilliant Corners Research, surveyed 1,000 likely voters by phone between August 23 and September 6. It found that concerns about democracy are also at a series high, with 76% of voters saying they believe democracy is under a major threat. At the same time, voters report high motivation to participate in the upcoming midterm elections, with 84% saying they plan to definitely vote in November.

Protecting the freedom to vote was rated as the top civil rights priority, receiving the highest importance rating among white, Black, Hispanic, and Asian American voters as well as among Democrats and Republicans. Overall, 14% of voters identified voting rights as their top issue, tying it with border security and ranking ahead of abortion rights, which 10% selected.

author: Sara Fayyazi
title: Addressing the Economic Costs of Sexual Violence: The Survivors’ Rights Restitution Act
content:
On September 15, 2026, Rep. Ayanna Pressley (MA-07), Rep. Teresa Leger Fernandez (NM-03), and Rep. Deborah Ross (NC-02) introduced the Survivors Rights Restitution Act. This legislation would establish a federal restitution program for survivors of sexual violence whose rights were violated by the federal government. The bill would include survivors of abuse by Jeffrey Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell while addressing the financial burden that can occur from sexual violence.

The bill focuses on the economic consequences that survivors can face long after an assault. The estimated lifetime cost of rape at $122,461 per victim, including the expenses of medical care, loss of income, housing instability and mental health support. These expenses can become an additional burden for survivors as they recover from trauma. The proposed restitution program would provide compensation for certain economic and non-economic harms and losses.

Under the legislation, an independent Office of Special Adjudicators for Survivors Restitution would be established within the US Court of Federal Claims. The office would review petitions from survivors and determine awards through what the bill describes as a streamlined, non-adversarial and trauma-informed process.
